items.title: Web engineering across two stacks
items.bodyMarkdown:
The V1 track walks from the mechanics of a single web request to a small, testable, secured feature that talks to a database. Twelve chapters, thirty-six lessons, three required exercises per lesson, and one placement check per chapter.

The track is deliberately linear. Every chapter assumes the vocabulary of the ones before it, and every chapter ends with a placement check whose items were written separately from the practice exercises, so passing it means the ideas transferred rather than that the answers were memorised.

The V2 chapters continue the same linear path into the problems that only appear once a feature has real data and real traffic: indexes and query plans, transactions that must not half-commit, API changes that do not break existing callers, work that happens outside a request, and the review and operational habits that keep all of it honest. They assume every V1 chapter.

The V3 chapters rebuild the same ground in C# and .NET. They are not a second beginners course: each one leans on what you already know from the Node chapters and spends its effort on what actually differs — a static type system you cannot opt out of, EF Core and the SQL it generates, concurrency tokens, ASP.NET Core authorization policies, and xUnit. The last chapter is explicitly comparative, because being able to say what is the same and what only looks the same is the point of learning the second stack.
items.description: A linear twelve-chapter path from the request/response cycle through JavaScript, TypeScript, the browser platform, React, Node.js APIs, relational data, authentication and day-to-day operation. Eight further chapters then go deeper: persistence and query plans, transaction correctness, safe API evolution, background work, security depth, database-backed integration testing, frontend depth, and operations and review. Ten final chapters rebuild the same work in C# and ASP.NET Core with EF Core, and compare the two stacks directly.
targetOutcomes: Explain what happens between a click in the browser and a rendered response.
Write and debug small JavaScript and TypeScript functions from evidence rather than guesswork.
Build an accessible React feature that reads and writes real server data.
Design a Node.js endpoint that validates input, scopes data to its owner and reports failures honestly.
Model, query and migrate relational data without losing or duplicating rows.
Ship a change with tests, logs and a rollback you have actually thought through.
Read a query plan and choose an index from evidence rather than habit.
Keep a multi-table invariant true under concurrent writes, and prove it.
Change a published API without breaking the callers already using it.
Run work outside the request cycle so that a retry does not duplicate its effects.
Build and test an equivalent ASP.NET Core service with EF Core, reading the SQL it generates.
Say what genuinely differs between the Node and .NET stacks, and what only looks different.
